title: AAV-MYO mediated overexpression of RBM20 in mice
projectDescription: Background Pathogenic variants in the RS domain of RBM20 cause dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) by impairing RBM20 nuclear import. Consequently, RBM20 accumulates in the cytoplasm in a form of cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates, and loses its splicing function. The relative contribution of these two processes to DCM pathogenesis remains unclear. Methods We used AAVMYO, a cardiomyocyte-specific adeno-associated virus gene transfer, to express FLAG-tagged murine Rbm20-R636Q driven by a cardiomyocyte-specific TnnT promoter in juvenile wild-type (WT) mice (named from here on AAV-mut, at low, medium and high doses). As a control, we administered high-dose AAV-mut to Rbm20-R636Q homozygous mice (DCM mice). We assessed survival, RBM20 expression and granule formation, cardiac stress markers, RBM20-dependent splicing, cardiac function, and integrated bulk RNA-sequencing, proteomics, and phospho-proteomics. Results In WT mice, low and medium AAV-mut doses were tolerated, whereas 75% of mice receiving the high dose died within 12 weeks. Medium-dose AAV-mut increased RBM20 protein ~1.5-fold, induced cytoplasmic RBM20 RNP condensates comparable to DCM mice, and upregulated cardiac stress markers Nppa/Nppb, while producing modest shifts in RBM20-dependent splicing toward DCM-like patterns. Echocardiography showed ventricular dilation and dose-dependent systolic dysfunction (reduced stroke volume, fractional shortening, and LVEF) without evidence of hypertrophy. In contrast, high-dose AAV-mut had minimal impact in DCM mice, with no additional stress marker induction, mis-splicing, or worsening of cardiac function. Multi-omics integration placed AAV-mut-treated WT hearts between WT and DCM hearts, with the largest shift in protein expression and comparatively mild phosphoproteomic changes. Shared programs in AAV-mut-treated WT and DCM hearts included extracellular matrix remodeling/cell-substrate adhesion and GTPase-mediated signaling, alongside broad repression of mitochondrial proteins involved in energy metabolism, including TMEM65. AAV-mut treatment in WT mice uniquely upregulated the immune/inflammatory program and the extrinsic apoptotic pathway but downregulated NFE2L2-oxidative stress response, while no changes were observed in treated DCM mice. Phosphoproteomics supported mild activation of CAMK2D-associated signaling. Conclusions Cytoplasmic RBM20 RNP condensates alone are sufficient to induce DCM-like ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction in WT hearts, even when RBM20-dependent splicing is partially preserved. The phenotype is associated with pronounced suppression of mitochondrial proteins and modest activation of CAMK2D-linked signaling, alongside induction of inflammatory and apoptotic programs. DCM hearts show limited additional deterioration upon further Rbm20-R636Q overexpression, suggesting increased tolerance to elevated levels of mutant RBM20.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cell lysis was performed essentially as described by Potel et al., 2025 (PMID: 39930009). Harvested cells were lysed in 4 M guanidinium isothiocyanate, 5 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP), 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide (CAA), 1% N-lauroylsarcosine, 5% isoamyl alcohol, and 40% acetonitrile in 125 mM HEPES pH 8.5. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 21,000 × g at room temperature. The resulting supernatant was transferred to a new tube and incubated for 1 hour at room temperature to ensure complete reduction and alkylation. Proteins were precipitated by adding three volumes of ice-cold 100% acetonitrile. Protein pellets were collected by centrifugation at 4,000 × g for 5 minutes, washed twice with 100% acetonitrile, followed by two additional washes with 70% ethanol. The protein pellets were digested with TPCK-treated trypsin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a ratio of 1:25 (w/w) at 37°C in 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) pH 8.5, overnight. Post-digestion, peptide concentrations were determined using a tryptophan assay (PMID: 25837572). Phosphopeptide enrichment was performed essentially as previously described by Leutert et al. (PMID: 37097255). Briefly, peptides were resuspended in IMAC loading solvent (80% acetonitrile, 0.4% TFA). Of each sample a small aliquot was used for full proteome analysis, while the remaining peptides were subjected to phosphopeptide enrichment using the KingFisher Apex™ platform (Thermo Fisher) and magnetic Fe-NTA beads (Cube Biotech). Enriched phosphopeptides were eluted with 0.2% dimethylamine in 80% acetonitrile to facilitate subsequent TMT labeling. Peptides (for the full proteome analysis) and the enriched phosphopeptides were labeled using TMTpro™ 18plex reagent as previously described (PMID: 33900084). Briefly, 0.5 mg of TMT reagent was dissolved in 45 µL of 100% acetonitrile. Subsequently, 4 µL of this solution was added to each peptide sample, followed by incubation at room temperature for 1 hour. The labeling reaction was quenched by adding 4 µL of a 5% aqueous hydroxylamine solution and incubating for an additional 15 minutes at room temperature. Labeled samples were then combined for multiplexing, desalted using an Oasis® HLB µElution Plate (Waters) according to the manufacturer's instructions, and dried by vacuum centrifugation. Combined TMT-labelled samples for the analysis of the input and the phosphoproteome were each subjected to offline high-pH reversed-phase fractionation (PMID: 22462785), which was carried out using an Agilent 1200 Infinity high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system, equipped with a Gemini C18 analytical column (3 μm particle size, 110 Å pore size, dimensions 100 x 1.0 mm, Phenomenex) and a Gemini C18 SecurityGuard pre-column cartridge (4 x 2.0 mm, Phenomenex). The mobile phases consisted of 20 mM ammonium formate adjusted to pH 10.0 (Buffer A) and 100% acetonitrile (Buffer B). The peptides were separated at a flow rate of 0.1 mL/min using the following linear gradient: 100% Buffer A for 2 minutes, ramping to 35% Buffer B over 59 minutes, increasing rapidly to 85% Buffer B within 1 minute, and holding at 85% Buffer B for an additional 15 minutes. Subsequently, the column was returned to 100% Buffer A and re-equilibrated for 13 minutes. During the LC separation, 48 fractions were collected. These were pooled into twelve fractions by combining every twelfth fraction. The pooled fractions were then dried using vacuum centrifugation.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw files were converted to mzML format using MSConvert from ProteoWizard, using peak picking, 64-bit encoding and zlib compression, and filtering for the 1000 most intense peaks. Files were then searched using MSFragger in FragPipe v23 (MSFragger version 4.3) against the FASTA database UP000000589 mus musculus (21968 entries; October 2022) containing common contaminants and reversed sequences. The following modifications were included into the search parameters: Carbamidomethylation (C, 57.0215), TMTpro (K, 304.2072) as fixed modifications; Oxidation (M, 15.9949), Acetylation (protein N-terminus, 42.0106), TMTpro (peptide N-terminus, 304.2072) as variable modifications. For the search of the phoshoproteome, phosporylation at STY (79.96633) was included and the number of allowed missed cleavages was set to 3 with a maximum number of variable modifications per peptide set to 5. For the full scan (MS1) a mass error tolerance of 20 PPM and for MS/MS (MS2) spectra of 20 PPM was set. For protein digestion, 'trypsin' was used as protease with an allowance of maximum 2 missed cleavages requiring a minimum peptide length of 7 amino acids. The false discovery rate on peptide and protein level was set to 0.01. For the proteomics data analysis the raw output files of FragPipe (protein.tsv files files) were processed using the R programming environment (ISBN 3-900051-07-0). Initial data processing included filtering out contaminants and reverse peptides. Only peptides quantified with at least 2 razor peptides (with Razor.Peptides >= 2) were considered for further analysis. 27077 peptides passed the quality control filters. In order to correct for technical variability, batch effects were removed using the 'removeBatchEffect' function of the limma package (PMID: 25605792) on the log2 transformed raw TMT reporter ion intensities ('channel' columns). Subsequently, normalization was performed using the 'normalizeVSN' function of the limma package (VSN - variance stabilization normalization - PMID: 12169536). Missing values were imputed with the 'knn' method using the 'impute' function from the Msnbase package (PMID: 22113085). This method estimates missing data points based on similarity to neighboring data points, ensuring that incomplete data did not distort the analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed using the moderated t-test provided by the limma package (PMID: 25605792). The model accounted for replicate information by including it as a factor in the design matrix passed to the 'lmFit' function. Imputed values were assigned a weight of 0.01 in the model, while quantified values were given a weight of 1, ensuring that the statistical analysis reflected the uncertainty in imputed data. A protein was considered differentially expressed if the log2 of its expression fold change was greater than 0.5, and if the fdr value was less than 0.05.
